title: Visa Uncertainty Is Making US Tech Workers Put Life Plans on Hold
excerpt: Tech workers on H-1B and student visas told Business Insider they are delaying purchases, weighing moves to Canada or the UK, and bracing for fewer sponsoring employers after IBM's sponsorship pullback and the PERM suspensions.
body:
• Tech visa holders told Business Insider that immigration policy uncertainty and job-security fears are shaping career decisions and long-term plans, with some delaying major purchases and others considering Canada or the UK.
  • IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in its consulting division, citing evolving skill availability and client needs, and workers fear other employers could follow.
  • In October the administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT services companies from the PERM program, a key step in the employment-based green card process; a proposed $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas has been blocked by federal courts.
  • What this means for you: no filing rule changed in this report — the practical risk is employer sponsorship. Workers on H-1B or STEM OPT should confirm their employer's current sponsorship policy before a job change or a large purchase tied to staying in the US.

Foreign tech workers in the United States are putting life decisions on hold — not because a single rule changed this week, but because several have moved at once. In interviews with Business Insider, workers on H-1B visas and student work permits described delaying purchases, tuning out the news, and quietly preparing exit options.

One tech worker on an F-1 STEM OPT visa said he has delayed buying a car because he does not know how long he will be able to remain in the US, and raised the possibility of moving to Canada or the UK. A Microsoft employee preparing for her final attempt at the H-1B lottery said that even if she is selected, the suspension of her employer from the green card process could block the next step.

"You can do everything right, build a career at a company like Microsoft, and still not feel secure about your future here."

— Microsoft employee interviewed by Business Insider

Who is affected, and by what

Three separate developments sit behind the anxiety. First, IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in its consulting division — a decision we reported separately in IBM's sponsorship pullback — with the company citing evolving skill availability and client needs. Kumar, a tech lead at a large corporation who in 2019 had to find a new sponsor inside the 60-day window after a job loss, told Business Insider he is concerned more companies could follow IBM's lead, shrinking the market for workers who need sponsorship.

Second, in October the Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT services companies from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program, a required step in most employment-based green card cases. The administration said the move aimed to stop companies favouring foreign workers over American workers; Microsoft has disputed allegations of misuse. Third, the administration has sought a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, a measure federal courts have blocked.

Not everyone is leaving

The report also found workers staying put. Aman Goyal, a product manager on an H-1B visa who came to the US in 2023, was laid off last year, considered looking for work abroad, and ultimately landed a new role in the Seattle area. For Goyal, the uncertainty has not outweighed the opportunities he sees in the US, and he is prioritising his network and his work in artificial intelligence. Another Big Tech visa holder said he is not too concerned because he does not have long-term immigration plans in the US.

What to do next

Nothing in this report changes a filing deadline. The exposure is at the employer level: sponsorship is a company policy, and it is changing company by company. Workers who would need a new sponsor after a layoff — H-1B holders generally have up to 60 days to find one — should know their current employer's sponsorship position, keep their status documents current, and treat large purchases that assume a long US stay as a decision to make with that risk in view.
